question: Xi Jinping out before 2027?
description:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if China's General Secretary of the Communist Party, Xi Jinping, is removed from power for any length of time between July 3, 2025, and December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No".

CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping will be considered removed from power if he announces his resignation from his role as General Secretary, or is otherwise dismissed, detained, disqualified, or otherwise loses his position or is prevented from fulfilling his duties as General Secretary within this market's timeframe.

The primary resolution source for this market will be a consensus of credible reporting.

eventMetadata.context_description: Xi Jinping's entrenched control over the Chinese Communist Party, Central Military Commission, and state institutions drives the 95.3% trader consensus against his removal before 2027. Ongoing military and party purges, including the recent sidelining of senior generals, have further centralized authority in loyal networks while eliminating potential rivals, with no designated successor emerging ahead of the 2027 Party Congress. Public appearances, diplomatic activity, and policy continuity through mid-2026 show no erosion of his position. While health events, elite factional challenges, or severe economic instability could theoretically shift dynamics within the resolution window, structural barriers and the absence of organized opposition sustain the market's assessment of continuity.

eventMetadata.context_description: The 2028 Democratic presidential nomination market remains tightly contested because the top three contenders—AOC, Gavin Newsom, and Jon Ossoff—sit within roughly three points of each other, reflecting an open field more than two years before primaries begin. With no incumbent president or clear party favorite, traders price in a wide range of potential paths through early-state contests, fundraising, and endorsements. Midterm results, state-level polling, and candidate positioning on economic policy, immigration, and party direction could quickly widen gaps.
